tracks.name: CSS Foundations
tracks.description: Selectors, properties, colors, and the box model.

lessons.title: 1. Inline and Internal CSS
lessons.summary: Two ways to add CSS directly to an HTML page.

activities.title: Adding color with a style attribute
activities.instruction: The simplest way to style an element is with the `style` attribute directly on the HTML tag. For multiple rules, use a `<style>` block in the `<head>`.
activities.example: Blue text

activities.title: Which takes priority?
activities.question: If you set `color: red` in a `<style>` block and `color: blue` on the element's `style` attribute, which color shows?
choices: Red, because the style block comes first
Blue, because inline styles override internal styles
They mix and become purple
activities.answer: Blue, because inline styles override internal styles
activities.explanation: Inline styles have higher specificity than style block rules. The browser always prefers the more specific declaration.

teaching.text: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls how HTML elements look. There are three ways to add CSS to a page, and we will start with the first two.
**Inline CSS** uses the `style` attribute on an element:
Red Heading
**Internal CSS** uses a `<style>` tag in the `<head>`:

<head>
  <style>
    h1 {
      color: red;
    }
  </style>
</head>
Internal CSS is better for styling multiple elements at once. Inline CSS is handy for quick, one-off fixes.
For real projects, you will use **external CSS** — a separate `.css` file linked with `<link>`. We will cover that later.

lessons.title: 2. Element and Class Selectors
lessons.summary: Targeting HTML elements with different selector types.

activities.title: Three selector types
activities.instruction: An **element selector** targets all instances of a tag. A **class selector** (prefixed with `.`) targets elements with a matching `class` attribute. An **ID selector** (prefixed with `#`) targets a single element with a matching `id`.

activities.title: How many elements styled?
activities.question:
Given `

One

Two

Three

` and the rule `.highlight { color: red; }`, how many paragraphs turn red?
choices: All three
Only the second one
None — classes don't work like that
activities.explanation: The `.highlight` selector only targets elements with `class="highlight"`. Only the second paragraph has that class.

teaching.text: Selectors tell the browser **which elements** to style. The most common types are:

Use **element selectors** when you want all instances of a tag to look the same. Use **class selectors** when you want to style a group of related elements. Use **ID selectors** for unique, one-of-a-kind elements.
In HTML, you apply classes and IDs like this:

This text is red.

This div has special styles.
Classes can be reused on many elements. IDs should only appear once per page. Prefer classes for styling — IDs are better used for JavaScript targeting and page anchors.

lessons.title: 3. Colors and Backgrounds
lessons.summary: Setting text and background colors with keywords, hex, and RGB.

activities.title: Color formats
activities.instruction: CSS accepts colors as named keywords, hex codes (`#RRGGBB`), or `rgb()` functions. All three work the same way — pick whichever is clearest for your use case.

activities.title: What color is #000000?
activities.question: What color does the hex code `#000000` represent?
choices: White
Black
Gray
activities.explanation: Hex `#000000` means zero red, zero green, zero blue — which is black. `#ffffff` (all channels maxed) is white.

teaching.text: The `color` property sets text color. The `background-color` property sets the background.
CSS supports several color formats:
You can also make backgrounds semi-transparent:

background-color: rgba(255, 0, 0, 0.5);  /* 50% transparent red */
background-color: hsla(200, 80%, 50%, 0.3);
The `background` shorthand property can set color, image, and position in one line: `background: #ff6347 url('img.png') no-repeat center;`

lessons.title: 4. The Box Model
lessons.summary: Every element is a box with content, padding, border, and margin.

activities.title: Anatomy of a box
activities.instruction: Every HTML element is a rectangular box. From inside out: **content** (text or image), **padding** (space inside the border), **border** (the edge), and **margin** (space outside the border).

activities.title: What goes where?
activities.question: If an element has `padding: 10px` and `border: 2px solid`, what is the total space from the outer edge of the border to the start of the content?
choices: 10px
12px
22px
activities.explanation: Padding (10px) + border (2px) = 12px from the outer edge of the border to the content. Margin is outside the border, so it doesn't count.

teaching.text: The box model is the most important CSS concept. Every element is a box with four layers:

content  →  padding  →  border  →  margin
(text)     (inner)      (edge)      (outer)
**`padding`** creates space between the content and the border. **`border`** is the visible edge. **`margin`** creates space between this element and its neighbors.
You can set each side individually or use shorthand:
By default, the `width` and `height` properties only set the content area. To include padding and border in the total width, use:
box-sizing: border-box;
Most developers apply `box-sizing: border-box` to all elements with a CSS reset. This makes sizing much more predictable.

lessons.title: 5. Typography
lessons.summary: Controlling fonts, sizes, weights, and line spacing.

activities.title: Setting up a font stack
activities.instruction: The `font-family` property sets the typeface. Always provide a fallback list — if the first font is unavailable, the browser tries the next one.

activities.title: What is a font stack?
activities.question: In `font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;`, what happens if Arial is not installed on the user's computer?
choices: The text has no font and doesn't display
The browser tries Helvetica, then falls back to the generic sans-serif
The browser downloads Arial automatically
activities.answer: The browser tries Helvetica, then falls back to the generic sans-serif
activities.explanation: Font stacks are tried in order. The generic family (`sans-serif`) is the final fallback that guarantees readable text.

teaching.text: Typography controls how text looks. The key properties are:
**`font-family`** sets the typeface. Always end with a generic family (`serif`, `sans-serif`, `monospace`) as a fallback.
**`font-size`** controls how large the text is. Common units: `px`, `em` (relative to parent), `rem` (relative to root).

h1 { font-size: 2rem; }     /* 2x the root size */
p  { font-size: 1rem; }     /* base size */
small { font-size: 0.875em; } /* 0.875x parent */
**`font-weight`** controls boldness: `400` is normal, `700` is bold, or use keywords `normal` and `bold`.
**`line-height`** sets the spacing between lines. A value of `1.5` to `1.6` is comfortable for body text.
For custom fonts, use `@font-face` or Google Fonts: `<link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Roboto&display=swap" rel="stylesheet">`

lessons.title: 6. Spacing and Sizing
lessons.summary: Controlling element dimensions and the space around them.

activities.title: Centering a fixed-width box
activities.instruction: Setting `margin: 0 auto` on a block element with a defined `width` centers it horizontally. The auto margins split the remaining space equally on both sides.

activities.title: Why auto?
activities.question: What does `margin: 0 auto` do to a 500px-wide div inside a 1000px-wide parent?
choices: Centers it with 250px margin on each side
Centers it with 250px margin on left and right (250px each)
It does nothing
activities.answer: Centers it with 250px margin on left and right (250px each)
activities.explanation: Remaining space = 1000 - 500 = 500px. `auto` splits it evenly: 250px left, 250px right.

teaching.text: You can control how much space an element takes up and how much room it has around it.
**`width` and `height`** set the content dimensions. Common values: `px`, `%`, `rem`, `vw` (viewport width).
**`margin: auto`** is the classic centering trick for block elements with a set width.
Margin can collapse — when two vertical margins touch, the browser uses the larger one, not the sum. This only happens vertically, never horizontally.

lessons.title: 7. Flexbox Basics
lessons.summary: Laying out items in a row or column with flexbox.

activities.title: A simple flex row
activities.instruction: Setting `display: flex` on a container makes its children lay out in a row by default. Use `justify-content` to distribute space along the main axis and `align-items` along the cross axis.

activities.title: What does gap do?
activities.question: In a flex container with `gap: 16px`, what is the space between each item?
choices: 16px on the left of each item only
16px between each pair of adjacent items
16px around every item on all sides
activities.answer: 16px between each pair of adjacent items
activities.explanation: `gap` adds consistent spacing between flex children without adding extra space at the edges.

teaching.text: Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout system. It arranges items in a row or a column and handles spacing, alignment, and sizing automatically.
**`justify-content`** distributes items along the main axis (horizontal in a row):

justify-content: flex-start;    /* packed to the left */
justify-content: center;        /* centered */
justify-content: space-between; /* equal space between items */
justify-content: space-around;  /* equal space around items */
**`align-items`** positions items along the cross axis (vertical in a row):

align-items: stretch;    /* fill container height */
align-items: center;     /* centered vertically */
align-items: flex-start; /* top */
align-items: flex-end;   /* bottom */
To stack items vertically, add `flex-direction: column`:
Flexbox also handles sizing with `flex-grow`, `flex-shrink`, and `flex-basis` — but `gap`, `justify-content`, and `align-items` cover most layout needs.

lessons.title: 8. CSS Grid Basics
lessons.summary: Two-dimensional layouts with rows and columns.

activities.title: A three-column grid
activities.instruction: CSS Grid creates a two-dimensional layout. Define columns with `grid-template-columns` and rows with `grid-template-rows`. Items fill cells automatically.

activities.title: What does 1fr mean?
activities.question: In `grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr 1fr`, what does `2fr` mean compared to `1fr`?
choices: It is twice as wide as a 1fr column
It is half as wide
fr means pixels, so it's 2px wide
activities.answer: It is twice as wide as a 1fr column
activities.explanation: `fr` stands for fraction. `2fr` takes twice the available space as `1fr`. The total space is divided into 4 parts (1+2+1), and each column gets its share.

teaching.text: CSS Grid is a two-dimensional layout system. It handles both rows and columns at once, making it perfect for page layouts and card grids.
The `fr` unit分配s available space as a fraction. `1fr 1fr 1fr` creates three equal columns.
You can also define explicit rows:

grid-template-rows: 60px 1fr 40px;
/* header: 60px, main: flexible, footer: 40px */
Grid items can span multiple columns or rows with `grid-column: span 2` or `grid-row: span 3`.

lessons.title: 9. Positioning
lessons.summary: Placing elements precisely with position properties.

activities.title: Position types in action
activities.instruction: `position: relative` offsets an element from its normal position. `position: absolute` removes it from flow and positions it relative to the nearest positioned ancestor. `position: fixed` pins it to the viewport.

activities.title: Fixed vs absolute
activities.question: What is the difference between `position: fixed` and `position: absolute`?
choices: Fixed stays in place when scrolling; absolute scrolls with the page
Absolute stays in place when scrolling; fixed scrolls with the page
They are the same thing
activities.answer: Fixed stays in place when scrolling; absolute scrolls with the page
activities.explanation: `fixed` is always relative to the viewport and stays put when the page scrolls. `absolute` is relative to the nearest positioned ancestor and scrolls with it.

teaching.text: CSS positioning lets you place elements exactly where you want them. There are four position values:

position: static;   /* default — normal flow */
position: relative; /* offset from normal position */
position: absolute; /* removed from flow, positioned relative to ancestor */
position: fixed;    /* removed from flow, positioned relative to viewport */
**`relative`** keeps the element in flow but lets you offset it with `top`, `right`, `bottom`, `left`.
**`absolute`** removes the element from the document flow. It positions relative to the nearest ancestor with `position: relative` (or any non-static value).

.parent { position: relative; }
.child  { position: absolute; top: 0; right: 0; }
**`fixed`** pins the element to the viewport. Perfect for sticky headers or floating buttons.
When you need an element to stay in the normal flow but act as a positioning context for absolute children, set `position: relative` on it — even without offset values.

lessons.title: 10. CSS Variables

activities.title: Defining and using variables
activities.instruction: CSS custom properties (variables) start with `--` and are accessed with `var()`. Define them on `:root` to make them available everywhere.

activities.title: Where to define?
activities.question:
If you define `--color: red` on a `
`, can a `

` inside that div use `var(--color)`?
choices: No, variables only work on the element they are defined on
Yes, child elements inherit custom properties from their parents
Only if you also define it on the p
activities.answer: Yes, child elements inherit custom properties from their parents
activities.explanation: Custom properties follow the cascade. They are inherited, so children can use variables defined on any ancestor.

teaching.text: CSS custom properties (variables) let you store values and reuse them throughout your stylesheet. They follow the cascade and are inherited by child elements.
Access them with `var()`. You can provide a fallback value as a second argument:

color: var(--primary);
background: var(--unknown, gray);  /* falls back to gray */
Variables can be overridden at any level, which is great for theming:
Custom properties are dynamic — you can change them with JavaScript: `element.style.setProperty('--primary', 'green')`.

lessons.title: 11. Transitions and Hover Effects
lessons.summary: Animating state changes smoothly with transitions.

activities.title: A smooth hover effect
activities.instruction: The `transition` property animates changes between states. Define which property to animate, how long it takes, and the timing function.

activities.title: What does ease do?
activities.question: In `transition: background 0.3s ease`, what does `ease` control?
choices: How long the transition takes
The speed curve of the animation (starts slow, speeds up, slows down at end)
Whether the transition repeats
activities.answer: The speed curve of the animation (starts slow, speeds up, slows down at end)
activities.explanation: `ease` is the default timing function — it starts slowly, accelerates in the middle, and decelerates at the end. Other options: `linear`, `ease-in`, `ease-out`, `ease-in-out`.

teaching.text: Transitions make state changes smooth instead of instant. You define the transition on the base state, and the browser animates to the hover/active/focus state.
Common timing functions:

linear          /* constant speed */
ease            /* default — slow start and end */
ease-in         /* slow start */
ease-out        /* slow end */
ease-in-out     /* slow start and end */
Popular properties to transition:

background-color  /* color changes */
color             /* text color changes */
transform         /* movement, scale, rotation */
opacity           /* fading in/out */
box-shadow       /* shadow effects */
For complex animations with multiple keyframes, use `@keyframes` instead of transitions. Transitions are best for simple two-state changes.

lessons.title: 12. Responsive Design
lessons.summary: Adapting layouts to different screen sizes.

activities.title: A media query in action
activities.instruction: Media queries let you apply CSS rules only when certain conditions are met — like the viewport being below a certain width. This is how sites adapt from desktop to mobile.

activities.title: Mobile-first vs desktop-first
activities.question: Which approach is generally recommended: writing styles for mobile first and adding `min-width` queries, or writing for desktop first and adding `max-width` queries?
choices: Desktop first with max-width
Mobile first with min-width (recommended)
It doesn't matter, they are equivalent
activities.explanation: Mobile-first means you write base styles for small screens and progressively enhance for larger ones. This tends to produce cleaner, more maintainable CSS.

teaching.text: Responsive design ensures your site looks good on all screen sizes — phones, tablets, and desktops.
The `@media` rule applies styles only when a condition is true:
Common breakpoints:
You can also query for other conditions like height, orientation, and color scheme:
Use `max-width` for desktop-first: `@media (max-width: 767px)` means 'only on screens smaller than 768px'.
